title: Lesson 7
subtitle: Locations — Where is it?
objectives: Say where an item is using doko, koko, soko and asoko
Learn the five simple rules for choosing between wa and ga
Connect two complete sentences with demo ('but')
Use the ii / yoi exception to say 'not good' (yokunai)
Say you are hungry, full, or thirsty
Read and write the hiragana ま み む め も

vocab.english: over there, that place over there

vocab.japanese: おなかがすいています
vocab.english: I'm hungry (literally: my stomach is empty)

vocab.japanese: おなかがいっぱいです
vocab.english: I'm full (literally: my stomach is full)

vocab.japanese: のどがかわいています
vocab.english: I'm thirsty (literally: my throat is dry)
Oh, I see / I got it

grammar.title: Using demo to connect two sentences
grammar.explanation: Demo ('but') is used to connect two complete sentences together. The second sentence begins with demo.

examples.japanese: フルーツは おいしいです。でも、おなかがいっぱいです。
examples.romaji: Furuutsu wa oishii desu. Demo, onaka ga ippai desu.
examples.english: Fruits are delicious. But I am full.

examples.japanese: のどがかわいています。でも、コーラは つめたくないです。
examples.romaji: Nodo ga kawaite imasu. Demo, koora wa tsumetakunai desu.
examples.english: I'm thirsty. But the cola isn't cold.

mistakes: Burying demo inside one sentence — it must start the second, complete sentence

grammar.title: Wa vs Ga rule #1: never wa after a question word
grammar.explanation: You can NEVER use wa directly after a question word. This is a simple rule with no exceptions. Use ga instead.

examples.japanese: なにが すきですか。
どれが いぬですか。

mistakes: Saying 'Nani wa suki desu ka' — wa can never follow a question word directly

grammar.title: Wa vs Ga rule #2: wa for comparison and emphasis
grammar.pattern: comparison or emphasis: [item] + wa (instead of ga)
grammar.explanation: Adjectives such as hoshii, suki and kirai normally use ga to mark the item being discussed. However, when comparing items or emphasizing, wa is used instead of ga.

examples.japanese: すいかは おいしいです。
examples.english: Watermelons are delicious. (emphasizing how tasty watermelons are)

examples.japanese: りんごが すきです。でも、バナナは きらいです。
examples.romaji: Ringo ga suki desu. Demo, banana wa kirai desu.
examples.english: I like apples. But I dislike bananas. (comparison)

examples.japanese: ねこが ほしくないです。でも、いぬは ほしいです。
examples.romaji: Neko ga hoshikunai desu. Demo, inu wa hoshii desu.
examples.english: I don't want a cat. But I want a dog. (comparison)

mistakes: Using ga when two items are being compared or emphasized — switch to wa

grammar.title: Wa vs Ga rule #3: both particles in the same sentence
grammar.explanation: Wa and ga can both be in the same sentence. Wa marks the topic and ga marks the object.

examples.japanese: わたしは ねこが すきです。
examples.romaji: Watashi wa neko ga suki desu.

examples.japanese: よしおさんは バナナが ほしいです。
examples.romaji: Yoshio san wa banana ga hoshii desu.

mistakes: Mixing them up: wa marks the topic, ga marks the object

grammar.title: Wa vs Ga rules #4 and #5: new topics and casual speech
grammar.pattern: new topic: [topic] + wa ... (casual speech: particles often dropped)
grammar.explanation: Rule #4: always use wa when introducing new topics of discussion; if the topic is restated or changed, use wa. Rule #5: wa and ga are often dropped in casual conversations, but until your Japanese is really good the book does not recommend dropping particles.

examples.english: I like cats. (particle dropped in casual speech)

mistakes: Dropping particles before your Japanese is really good

grammar.title: The ii / yoi exception
grammar.pattern: not good: yoi + kunai = yokunai (not iku nai)
grammar.explanation: Both ii and yoi mean 'nice, good'. In Lesson 6 you learned to make adjectives negative by dropping i and adding kunai, but ii is an exception: although you may hear iku nai in casual conversation, it is not standard. Use yokunai to say 'not good'.

grammar.title: The doko word group: asking and answering where
grammar.pattern: [item] wa doko desu ka / koko desu, soko desu, asoko desu
grammar.explanation: Doko asks 'where? what place?'. Answers use koko (here), soko (there), asoko (over there), soto (outside) or naka (inside). The Lesson 2 ko-so-a-do diagram applies to these distance relationships. When a question word like doko is the subject, use ga: 'Doko ga ii desu ka.'

examples.japanese: いぬは どこですか。
いぬは あそこです。
どこが いいですか。

mistakes: Using koko for something far away — asoko is for 'that place over there'

grammar.title: Hiragana ま み む め も
grammar.pattern: ma = ま, mi = み, mu = む, me = め, mo = も
grammar.explanation: The fifth row of hiragana. Learn the correct stroke order since correct stroke order will mean neater characters when writing quickly.

examples.english: to read — everyday word using む
a drink — everyday word using の, み, も

mistakes: Ignoring stroke order — it makes quick writing sloppy

Koko desu ka = Is it here?

おなかがいっぱいです
quiz.explanation: Onaka ga ippai desu literally means 'my stomach is full' = I'm full.

quiz.explanation: Demo starts the second sentence; ookii = big.

summary: Doko asks where; koko, soko and asoko answer here, there and over there (plus soto and naka). Demo ('but') starts the second of two complete sentences. Wa can never follow a question word directly — use ga; wa otherwise marks topics, emphasis and comparisons, while ga marks the object. Ii becomes yokunai (not ikunai) for 'not good'. Onaka ga suite imasu = I'm hungry; onaka ga ippai desu = I'm full; nodo ga kawaite imasu = I'm thirsty. New hiragana: ま み む め も.
